svg.title: An RTO has to be split into a time budget with an owner per segment, or the drill measures improvisation
svg.desc: A bank promised an RTO of two hours. The exercise took nine hours; the network switchover itself was twenty-five minutes and the remaining eight hours and thirty-five minutes went to waiting for business authorisation, draining the storage replication backlog, unsynchronised DNS and certificates, and business validation without executable test cases. The design had written down only the segment it controlled.
svg.text: The design wrote down the twenty-five minutes it controlled; the other eight hours were never in the document
Promised RTO 2 h, RPO 15 min. The annual exercise measured 9 h of downtime and about 40 min of lost transactions
TARGET · the RTO must be a budget with an owner per segment, not a single number
detect
5 min
authorise
who decides, in what time?
network switch
25 min, measured
storage catch-up
depends on the backlog
app start
start order matters
business validation
needs test cases, not a login
sum must be ≤ 2 h — otherwise lower the commitment or fund the gap
WHAT THE DRILL MEASURED · 9 h, of which 8 h 35 min had no owner
waiting for business confirmation · draining replication backlog · DNS and certificates unsynchronised ·
business validation with no executable cases · nobody authorised to decide
the part the network team measured
The gap is not a network failure. It is a definition failure: business reads RTO as "business restored",
the network team reads it as "links switched", and the difference was never written down by anyone.
What the design must add
automated DNS, certificate and configuration sync to the DR site · independent, bandwidth-guaranteed
replication path · pre-switch health checks · the ability to switch partially, core first
The single most important line: put the decision time limit for "business confirmation" into the design document. An RTO without an authorisation deadline is never met.
Remediation methodology: phase gates for the audit trail (assess, design, implement, exercise, sign-off) while the individual fixes move across a Kanban board week by week.
